title: From clay pots to pink pigs: the piggy bank's long history
description: The piggy bank is named after neither a farmer nor a fairy tale. Its story starts with an orange clay called pygg — and a misunderstanding that gave savings a snout.

body.heading: Pots made of pygg
paragraphs: In medieval England, people kept coins in pots made from an inexpensive orange clay called pygg. A 'pygg pot' was simply a clay money jar — to reach the coins, you had to smash it, which made it a stern little savings device.
By the 18th century the clay's name had faded, and potters hearing 'pygg bank' began shaping the pots as pigs. The pun stuck, and the pig became the world's symbol of saving.

body.heading: Why the design still works
paragraphs: The classic piggy bank teaches the oldest savings lesson in the world: money you cannot easily reach is money you do not spend. Having to break the pot — or at least stop and think — adds friction exactly where impulse wants speed.
Modern versions with plugs trade a little of that friction for reusability. The lesson survives either way: separate the money, make it visible, and let it accumulate undisturbed.

takeaway: Piggy banks began as pots of 'pygg' clay that had to be smashed to open — potters turned the name into pigs, and the friction became the lesson.
